textContent.text: In the dense Amazon rainforest, a bright green trail winds over twisting roots, under low ferns, and across the forest floor. From a distance, it looks like a procession of thousands of green-winged butterflies. A closer look, however, reveals the truth: The moving "wings" are actually fragments of leaves carried by ants marching in perfect formation. These are leafcutter ants, and they're toting the leaves back to their nest—not to eat, but to fertilize their fungus farm.

They are best known for cutting pieces of leaves and carrying them back to their nests in trails that can stretch for more than a hundred feet. Once there, leafcutters plant the leaves in special chambers that house their primary source of food: a soft, white fungus called
, which grows in spongy mats along the floors and walls.
The process of cultivating the fungus is shared among different members of the colony, each with a specific role. Foraging ants called
leave the nest to collect fresh leaves, often guarded by larger
that protect them from predators. Inside the nest, smaller

take over, chewing the leaves into a soft pulp, forming the pulp into pellets, and planting the pellets among the fungus. The pellets act as fertilizer, with the fungus breaking them down and absorbing their nutrients as it grows.

textContent.text: Leafcutter ants have developed multiple ways to keep their fungal gardens safe and healthy. While the maxima ants defend the colony from outside predators, the smaller workers act as internal caretakers. Some serve as garbage collectors, removing used leaf fragments, dead ants, and other detritus that could attract harmful organisms. Other ants crawl through the fungal beds spreading a naturally produced bacteria that works like weed-killer for potential parasites. Together, these countermeasures protect the colony's crop from a number of different pathogens that could infect and spoil it.

The regulated temperature, humidity, and airflow inside the ants' nest create stable conditions that the fungus could never find on its own. Additionally, as the ants feed on the fungus, their waste returns helpful enzymes to the gardens, which continue breaking down new leaves and adding nutrients to the fungal bed.

Leafcutter ants and their cultivated fungus form one of nature's most extraordinary partnerships. title.text: The Massive Challenge of Tiny Plastics

textContent.text: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean lies a floating mass of debris known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Spanning an area twice the size of Texas, it has become a symbol of how much plastic waste humanity has produced. Yet the mountains of bottles and bags drifting on the surface represent only the most visible part of the problem. Far more dangerous is what cannot be seen—tiny fragments of plastic, called microplastics, that reach the ocean in many ways and are nearly impossible to remove.

Most microplastics begin as larger pieces of plastic litter in the ocean, much of which is washed off streets by rain and carried out to sea through storm drains and rivers. Once there, waves, sunlight, and salt water break down the litter into smaller and smaller fragments until many are too tiny to be seen by the naked eye. Scientists estimate that a single plastic bottle can eventually splinter into tens of thousands of microplastic particles.

Other microplastics enter the ocean already broken down. Synthetic fabrics such as polyester or artificial fleece release microscopic fibers whenever they are washed. These fibers flow into sewer systems but are too small for water treatment plants to filter out, so they pass through with wastewater and eventually reach rivers that flow into the ocean. Car tires also shed plastic particles as they wear down on the road, and rainfall can wash those particles into gutters and storm drains. Once there, they too can be carried to the sea.

Coming from so many sources, microplastics have disseminated through the world's oceans, affecting marine ecosystems from shallow coral reefs to the deepest sea floors. Marine animals are often the first victims of this contamination; because the particles are so small, many animals ingest them, mistaking the larger fragments for food or accidentally swallowing smaller fragments with their food. Once inside an animal's stomach, they can cause the animal to feel full, preventing it from getting enough nutrients. As they are digested, microplastics may also release harmful chemicals that can build up in tissues and move through the food chain as one animal eats another. Over time, these particles tend to accumulate at the top of the food chain and have even been found in humans.

Currently, the main approach to tackling the microplastics problem is prevention. Many countries have banned or limited single-use plastic products, such as shopping bags and drinking straws, in hopes of cutting down on plastic litter. Some modern washing machines now come with filters that trap microfibers before they enter wastewater, and many wastewater treatment plants are also beginning to use membrane bioreactor systems, which can capture smaller particles that older filtration systems might miss. Together, these measures aim to reduce the creation of new microplastics and limit how much ultimately reaches the ocean.

Still, these efforts address only part of the problem. Scientists are experimenting with cleanup technologies—from magnetic fluids that draw plastic fragments out of wastewater to specialized trawling vessels that skim them from the sea's surface. However, these technologies are still many years away from being practical for large-scale use. For now, the best defense against microplastics may be to use and discard less plastic in the first place. Every plastic item that stays out of landfills, rivers, and oceans helps slow the spread of microplastic pollution.

title.text: Huge dust storm hits Kansas during the Dust Bowl, an agricultural, ecological, and economic disaster in the Great Plains region of North America in the 1930s
Black Sunday

textContent.text: Sunday, April 14, 1935 began as a beautiful day in America's southern Great Plains. The air was warm and still, and the wide, open prairie stretched under a cloudless sky. Then, an ominous dark-gray cloud appeared to the north. Those who stopped to watch the churning mass saw an enormous, menacing wall of dust moving steadily closer, blotting out the sun and swallowing the landscape. It was a sight so terrifying that people would forever remember the day as Black Sunday.

The storm stretched nearly eight hundred miles across Nebraska, eastern Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, and the Texas Panhandle, with winds up to eighty-five miles per hour carrying millions of tons of dry topsoil. Although it was midday, the sky turned black, and people could not see their own hands in front of their faces. Many who were caught outside became lost or stranded as the storm raged around them. Some thought the world itself was ending.

Although the southern plains had long experienced dry weather and powerful wind storms, the land's thick native grasses had previously protected the soil by holding it in place. That natural protection began to disappear after the Homestead Act of 1862, which brought thousands of settlers west and turned much of the prairie into farmland. Over the next several decades, farmers plowed up the soil and replaced the native plants with wheat and cotton, crops that quickly drained the soil of nutrients and left it vulnerable to erosion. When a severe drought struck in the early 1930s, the worn-out soil could no longer hold moisture or resist the wind. Without the deep roots of native grasses to anchor it, the dry earth broke apart, and powerful gusts lifted the loose topsoil into the air, creating enormous dust storms that swept across the region.

As the drought dragged on and the storms grew stronger, daily life on the southern plains changed. To keep the dirt out of their homes, people sealed windows and doors with wet rags, but it was impossible to stop the dust entirely. When the winds died down, households had to shovel the dust away from their doors, sweep it off their floors, and strain it from milk and water. Many wore cloths over their faces to avoid breathing it in, and parents covered babies' cribs with damp sheets for protection. Even with these precautions, however, thousands suffered from dust pneumonia—a lung disease caused by inhaling fine particles of soil—and many did not survive.

Between 1932 and 1934, there were dozens of major dust storms across the southern plains, but it was Black Sunday's storm—the most violent of them all—that would go on to define the era. When a newspaper reporter described the event, he called the region it struck the "dust bowl." The phrase quickly caught on and eventually became the name historians use for this years-long ecological disaster. Black Sunday also convinced many Americans that the government needed to take action. Within weeks, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Soil Conservation Act, a law that encouraged farmers to use new plowing and planting methods to protect the soil from erosion. These efforts gradually helped restore the grasslands of the southern Great Plains and prevent future storms from being as devastating as Black Sunday.

title.text: Microgravity and the Body

textContent.text: Have you ever seen video clips of astronauts in space torpedoing through corridors or turning somersaults in mid-air? They can do these things because of microgravity, a state of greatly reduced gravity that makes people and objects nearly weightless. Living in conditions of microgravity may look like fun, but researchers have long observed its serious effects on the human musculoskeletal system.

On Earth, the invisible force of gravity pulls our bodies and everything around us toward the ground. As we perform everyday actions like walking, wearing a backpack, or picking up a ball, our muscles and bones work together to resist this force. In turn, this regular work helps keep our muscles and bones strong. However, astronauts living in microgravity experience the opposite effect: Once released from gravity's constant pull, their muscles weaken and their bones begin to break down.

Under normal conditions, bone tissue constantly renews itself, with old or damaged cells replaced by new ones. In microgravity, the body continues to remove old or damaged bone tissue, but the formation of new tissue slows dramatically. Because bones are constantly being broken down faster than they are rebuilt, they begin to lose calcium and other minerals that give them strength. This process occurs naturally as people age on Earth, but in space it happens much more rapidly. For a typical six-month mission aboard the International Space Station, astronauts typically lose 6% to 9% of their bone density, a rate nearly ten times that of age-related bone loss on Earth.

When muscles are not used regularly, they lose mass and strength over time. It can happen to anyone—for example, when a person is bedridden or has a broken limb in a cast. In space, this atrophy happens much faster. When the body's muscles aren't required to work as hard as they do in Earth's gravity, the body begins breaking down muscle proteins faster than it builds new ones. This kind of atrophy is especially prominent in the muscles of the legs, back, and neck—the ones used to keep our bodies upright on Earth—since the absence of gravity means they no longer bear a person's weight.

Loss of muscle mass and bone density don't normally cause problems while in space, but they can cause issues when astronauts return to Earth. When they land, astronauts often have to be carried away from their spacecraft on stretchers or chairs, in part because their weakened muscles and bones can't immediately support their body weight. To recover, they must undergo weeks or even months of physical rehabilitation to rebuild strength, restore bone density, and retrain their bodies to move in normal gravity again.

To reduce the physical decline caused by microgravity and shorten recovery periods, astronauts follow carefully designed routines to maintain muscle and bone health while in space. One of the ways they do this is by exercising an average of two hours a day using special equipment built for microgravity workouts. Astronauts also take nutritional supplements, like calcium and vitamin D to help replace the minerals that bones lose in space.

These countermeasures allow astronauts to minimize the harms of microgravity, but they can't eliminate the problem entirely. With space agencies around the world planning missions to Mars, future astronauts may be living in space for longer than ever before. For this reason, scientists continue working diligently to understand how the human body responds to microgravity in order to keep astronauts healthy and prepare them for the challenges of deep space exploration.

title.text: The Mystery of the Monarchs

textContent.text: Every autumn, hundreds of millions of monarch butterflies abandon their summer habitats in the eastern regions of the United States and Canada to travel south for winter. People have known about the butterflies' migration for centuries, but it was not until the 1970s that scientists were finally able to confirm where they spent their winters and how far they traveled to get there. The mystery was solved by a Canadian zoologist named Fred Urquhart who tracked the monarchs' movements in a remarkable research effort that spanned nearly forty years.

When he began his investigation in 1937, Urquhart needed to design an effective way to follow the insects. Migrating birds had been successfully tracked by placing small bands around their legs; however, a monarch's legs are too thin and delicate to make this approach practical. Urquhart tried using paint and ink to write identifying information on the butterflies' wings, but the markings blended into the monarch's already-colorful patterns.

After nearly five years of experimentation, Urquhart finally found a workable solution. He used a strong but harmless adhesive to affix tiny paper stickers to the monarchs' wings—secure enough to survive wind and rain, but light enough that the butterflies could still fly freely. Printed on each sticker was a code showing where the butterfly had been tagged, along with Urquhart's address. Throughout the 1940s, Urquhart and his wife, Norah, released thousands of tagged monarchs into the wild, hoping that reports from recovered butterflies would help them trace the insects' long migration route.

By the early 1950s, Urquhart's tagging project was beginning to show promising results, but he needed help. In 1952, he published an article describing his work and asking the public to help expand it. Thousands of volunteers across North America joined the effort, tagging monarchs in their own communities so the migration could be tracked on a much larger scale. But by the mid-1960s—nearly thirty years after his search began—Urquhart still could not explain where the hundreds of millions of migrating butterflies were going. His data showed a clear pattern of southward movement and sightings across the southern United States, yet their ultimate wintering grounds remained unknown to him.

Over the years, as Urquhart plotted the incoming data on a map, an emerging pattern pointed to Mexico as a likely destination. He enlisted the help of Kenneth Brugger and Catalina Aguado, both residents of Mexico who had read one of Urquhart's articles and responded to his request for volunteers. The couple drove around areas identified as potential butterfly habitats, speaking with local townspeople. People have known about the butterflies' migration for centuries, but it was not until the 1970s that scientists were finally able to confirm where they spent their winters and how far they traveled to get there. The mystery was solved by a Canadian zoologist named Fred Urquhart who tracked the monarchs' movements in a remarkable research effort that spanned nearly forty years.

When he began his investigation in 1937, Urquhart needed to design an effective way to follow the insects. Migrating birds had been successfully tracked by placing small bands around their legs; however, a monarch's legs are too thin and delicate to make this approach practical. Urquhart tried using paint and ink to write identifying information on the butterflies' wings, but the markings blended into the monarch's already-colorful patterns.

After nearly five years of experimentation, Urquhart finally found a workable solution. He used a strong but harmless adhesive to affix tiny paper stickers to the monarchs' wings—secure enough to survive wind and rain, but light enough that the butterflies could still fly freely. Printed on each sticker was a code showing where the butterfly had been tagged, along with Urquhart's address. Throughout the 1940s, Urquhart and his wife, Norah, released thousands of tagged monarchs into the wild, hoping that reports from recovered butterflies would help them trace the insects' long migration route.

By the early 1950s, Urquhart's tagging project was beginning to show promising results, but he needed help. In 1952, he published an article describing his work and asking the public to help expand it. Thousands of volunteers across North America joined the effort, tagging monarchs in their own communities so the migration could be tracked on a much larger scale. But by the mid-1960s—nearly thirty years after his search began—Urquhart still could not explain where the hundreds of millions of migrating butterflies were going. His data showed a clear pattern of southward movement and sightings across the southern United States, yet their ultimate wintering grounds remained unknown to him.

Over the years, as Urquhart plotted the incoming data on a map, an emerging pattern pointed to Mexico as a likely destination. He enlisted the help of Kenneth Brugger and Catalina Aguado, both residents of Mexico who had read one of Urquhart's articles and responded to his request for volunteers. Their inquiries led them to central Mexico's Sierra Madre mountains, where the monarchs were well known to local residents, who looked forward to the butterflies' arrival each autumn.
